title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
short: Particles move in every state; the states differ in how close the particles are and how freely they move.
trouble: Students think the particles in a solid do not move at all, or that the particles themselves swell, melt or boil when heated.

blocks.html: Water can be ice, liquid or steam, yet the molecules are the same $\mathrm{H_2O}$ in all three. Elements, Compounds and Mixtures sorted matter by what it is made of; here we sort it by how its particles are arranged and how they move. The particle model says that matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving and that attract each other.

In a solid, particles are packed close and vibrate about fixed positions. In a liquid, they are still close but slide past each other. In a gas, they are far apart and fly freely in straight lines between collisions. Heating makes the particles move faster; it does not make them bigger.

Two things compete: the attractions between particles, which pull them together, and their motion, which pulls them apart. When motion is weak compared with the attractions, the particles are held in place (solid). With more energy they can roll past each other but stay touching (liquid). With enough energy they break free completely (gas). That is why a solid keeps its shape, a liquid keeps its volume but flows, and a gas fills any container and can be squeezed: most of a gas is empty space.

blocks.title: Reading melting and boiling points
blocks.q: At 1 atm, ethanol melts at $-114\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and boils at $78\ ^\circ\text{C}$. What state is ethanol in at $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$? At $-120\ ^\circ\text{C}$?
steps: Below the melting point: solid. Between the melting and boiling points: liquid. Above the boiling point: gas.

blocks.title: A warm iron bar
blocks.q: An iron bar grows slightly longer when heated. What happens to its atoms?
steps: Heating gives the atoms more kinetic energy, so they vibrate faster and harder.
Harder vibration pushes neighbors a little farther apart on average, so the bar expands.
The atoms themselves keep their size.
blocks.a: They vibrate faster and sit slightly farther apart; they do not grow.

blocks.html: Thinking that particles in a solid do not move, or that particles swell, melt or boil themselves. A single molecule has no state: "melting" describes how a crowd of molecules is arranged. Check your picture against an everyday fact: a solid warms up, which means its particles gain motion, so they must have been moving already.
Try it in Gas in a Box: heat the gas and watch the particles speed up while their size stays the same.
